Traditional Likert scales, the preferred choice for many psychology researchers, come with notable limitations: predefined response options that constrain responses, careless responding, debates about whether response categories are truly equidistant, and susceptibility to common method bias, which can inflate relationships. title: From Text to Predictions: Using LLMs for NLP Tasks
text:
🧠 Generating Text-embeddings From Texts
Text embeddings are a fundamental NLP technique that transforms textual data into numerical vectors, making it digestible for processing by Machine Learning (ML) models (Ma et al., 2019). These embeddings and their large dimensions encapsulate the semantic, syntactic, and contextual properties of the text in a format that can be processed efficiently by computers.

Tokenization
The first step to transform the texts into text-embeddings is tokenization. Tokenization, a fundamental preprocessing step in natural language processing (NLP), involves segmenting text into smaller units called tokens (Bird et al., 2009). Tokens are essentially segments of the text that are treated as distinct units for analysis, typically words or subwords. For example, word-level tokenization would split “Natural language processing is fascinating” into [“Natural”, “language”, “processing”, “is”, “fascinating”]. Modern tokenization methods typically utilize subwords due to their increased utility.
Before tokenization, establishing a consistent token size across all data points is beneficial. This standardization allows LLMs to process text and generate embeddings more efficiently. I prefer setting the token size to accommodate the longest responses to avoid data loss, with shorter responses padded to match. Alternatively, using the average token length is possible, but this approach risks truncating longer responses and losing data.
# Calculate the length of each text entry in tokens
token_lengths = []  # List to store token counts
for text in df['text_variable']: # change 'text_variable' to the variable in your dataset
    token_lengths.append(len(text.split()))

max_token = max(token_lengths)
min_token = min(token_lengths)

# Print the shortest and longest tokenized responses
print("Shortest response (in tokens):", max_token)
print("Longest response (in tokens):", max_token)


Text-embeddings
After tokenization, the resulting tokens are fed into a pre-trained model (e.g., BERTBASE) to generate text embeddings. These embeddings are high-dimensional vectors; for BERTBASE, the output is a (sample_size, 768) matrix, while for BERTLARGE, it’s (sample_size, 1024). Several strategies exist for utilizing these outputs. Embeddings can be extracted from a single layer (out of 12 for BERTBASE and 24 for BERTLARGE) or by concatenating or averaging embeddings from multiple layers. Extracting from the last layer, the second-to-last layer, and averaging or concatenating the last four layers has proven particularly effective for various NLP tasks (Devlin et al., 2018; Kjell et al., 2023). The code snippet below provides an example of a function that generates text embeddings by averaging the output of the last four hidden layers.
# Function for text-embeddings that encode the average of last four hidden layers
def mean_of_last_four_layers(text):

    # Tokenize text and convert to tensor
    encoded_input = tokenizer(text, max_length=max_token, padding='max_length', truncation=True, return_tensors='pt')

    # Forward pass, disable gradient calculation
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = bert(**encoded_input)
        hidden_states = outputs.hidden_states

    # Stack the last four layers and calculate the mean along the new dimension (0)
    last_four_layers = torch.stack((hidden_states[-4], hidden_states[-3], hidden_states[-2], hidden_states[-1]))
    mean_embeddings = torch.mean(last_four_layers, dim=0)

    return mean_embeddings.squeeze().numpy()

# Apply the function to the 'text_variable' column
df['encoded'] = df['text_variable'].apply(lambda x: mean_of_last_four_layers(x))
As an alternative to averaging the last four hidden layers, you can extract the output from a specific layer. For instance, to use the second-to-last layer (layer 11 in BERTBASE), use the following code:
# Function for embeddings from a specific BERT layer
def encode_text(text, layer_index):

    # Tokenize text and convert to tensor
    encoded_input = tokenizer(text, max_length = max_token, padding = 'max_length', truncation=True, return_tensors='pt')

    # Forward pass, disable gradient calculation
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = bert(**encoded_input)
        hidden_states = outputs.hidden_states

    # Select the embeddings from the specified layer
    return hidden_states[layer_index].squeeze().numpy()

# 11th layer (second to last)
# Change this to get embeddings from a different layer
selected_layer = 11

# Encode the column (this example directly updates the DataFrame)
df['encoded_layer_11'] = df['text_variable'].apply(lambda x: encode_text(x, layer_index=selected_layer))

title: From Text to Predictions: Using LLMs for NLP Tasks
text:
🤖 Fitting Text-embeddings into ML Models
To use text embeddings in regression or machine learning models, you can perform mean pooling, reducing the three-dimensional token embeddings (sample_size, token_size, 768) to two-dimensional vectors (sample_size, 768). This process averages the embeddings across all tokens per document/data point, creating a single vector representing the overall semantic content of individual responses. While mean pooling might lose some contextual nuances, it balances detail with computational efficiency, effectively filtering noise and ensuring no single token overly influences the model (Biggiogera et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019; Maini et al., 2020). You will then use these mean embeddings as input features for different ML models.
# Splitting the dataset into training and testing sets
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

# Converting the 'encoded' column to a numpy array and averaging across tokens
train_embeddings = np.array(train_df['encoded'].tolist())
x_train = np.mean(train_embeddings, axis=1)

test_embeddings = np.array(test_df['encoded'].tolist())
x_test = np.mean(test_embeddings, axis=1)

# Converting the target variable column to a numpy array
y_train = np.array(train_df['target_variable'].tolist())
y_test = np.array(test_df['target_variable'].tolist())

# Initializing the regression model
rf_regressor = RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42) # to use a different ML model change this line

# Training the model
rf_regressor.fit(x_train, y_train)

# Making predictions on the test set
test_predictions = rf_regressor.predict(x_test)

# Evaluating the model
mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, test_predictions)
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, test_predictions)
cor = np.corrcoef(y_test, test_predictions)

# Displaying evaluation metrics
print(f'Mean Squared Error (MSE): {mse:.4f}')
print(f'Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): {rmse:.4f}')
print(f'R-squared (R²): {r2:.4f}')
print(f'Correlation Coefficient: {cor[0, 1]:.4f}')

K-fold Cross-validation
# Convert the 'encoded' column to a numpy array and average across tokens
embeddings = np.array(df['encoded'].tolist())
x_input = np.mean(embeddings, axis=1)

# Convert the target variable column to a numpy array
input_y = np.array(df['target_variable'].tolist())  # Replace 'target_variable' with the actual column name

# Initialize the Random Forest regressor
regressor = RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42)

# K-Fold Cross-Validation setup
kfold = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

# Cross-validation: Calculate Negative Mean Squared Error (converted to RMSE)
mse_scores = cross_val_score(regressor, x_input, input_y, cv=kfold, scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
mean_rmse = np.mean(np.sqrt(-mse_scores))
print(f'Mean Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): {mean_rmse:.4f}')

# Cross-validation: Calculate R-squared (R²) scores
r2_scores = cross_val_score(regressor, x_input, input_y, cv=kfold, scoring='r2')
mean_r2 = np.mean(r2_scores)
print(f'Mean R-squared (R²): {mean_r2:.4f}')

# Cross-validation: Generate predictions for each fold
predictions = cross_val_predict(regressor, x_input, input_y, cv=kfold)

# Calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient
correlation, _ = pearsonr(input_y, predictions)
print(f'Correlation Coefficient: {correlation:.4f}')

title: From Text to Predictions: Using LLMs for NLP Tasks
text:
💭 Conclusion
In this blog post, I demonstrated how to leverage pre-trained LLMs like BERT for NLP tasks, covering text tokenization, embedding extraction, and their application in predictive ML models. We explored techniques such as averaging or selecting embeddings from specific hidden layers to balance computational efficiency and contextual richness. We also showed how to integrate these embeddings into ML pipelines, including training, prediction and evaluation using RMSE, R², and k-fold cross-validation. Using LLM-based embeddings for feature engineering allows models to capture nuanced textual relationships, empowering solutions for text classification, sentiment analysis, and other NLP challenges.
I hope this post provided a helpful starting point for using LLMs to analyze large amounts of unstructured text data for prediction. With further exploration, you’ll be ready to tackle more advanced techniques, including using regression heads directly on LLMs, fine-tuning models for specific tasks, and utilizing LLMs pre-trained on specialized corpora.Feel free to connect and share your progress and research.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
text:
Upskilling workers has become essential in today’s rapidly evolving work landscape. The shift is undeniable—work is changing right before our eyes. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated this transformation, pushing professionals across industries to adapt to a fully digital world. Teachers pivoted to virtual classrooms, professionals mastered remote collaboration tools, and platforms like Zoom, Slack, and Microsoft Teams became indispensable. How did we prepare for this sudden shift? Through resources, support, resilience and, crucially training. Then, as workers settled into the comfort of remote work—attending meetings in pajama pants—companies began calling them back to the office. The challenge? Many employees had grown unaccustomed to in-person collaboration, and some even resisted returning entirely. For tech companies, this led to layoffs of workers reluctant to re-enter the office environment. How did organizations ease this transition? Through incentives, but also through training.
Fast forward to the present, where the rise of generative AI is reshaping industries. Initially, fears of job displacement loomed, but soon we discovered AI’s potential to enhance productivity—provided we fact-check its output and manage its “hallucinations.” And once again, training became the bridge to mastering this new era of work. Training isn’t just about adapting to change or upskilling; it has long been a trusted solution for tackling organizational and management challenges. For generations, consultants have relied on training to solve problems, foster growth, and drive innovation. It’s not just a tool; it’s the go-to strategy for navigating the complexities of the modern workplace.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
section: 📈 The Training Industry: Current Trends and Challenges
text:
📈 The Training Industry: Current Trends and Challenges
The Training and Development industry, valued at an astonishing $352.66 billion (Business Wire, 2024), continues to grow rapidly. Despite its size, the industry grapples with a persistent challenge: transfer of training—the extent to which skills learned in a training program are applied effectively in the workplace to solve real-world problems (Blume et al., 2010). Shockingly, the success rate of training transfer remains at just 10-22% (Connolly, 2021). For organizations investing billions into training, this statistic highlights a critical gap and underscores the potential for improvement.
While training is an effective method to address various organizational issues, it is not always the appropriate solution. The specific problem at hand and the context of the organization play critical roles in training success. This is why a needs assessment is necessary to determine whether training is indeed the solution to a given problem. When implemented appropriately, training can be highly impactful.






In this blog post, I share some takeaways from Blume et al.’s (2010) meta-analysis—one of the most insightful and impactful studies I’ve encountered. This research sheds light on the key factors that contribute to effective training transfer, offering valuable guidance for consultants and organizations striving to maximize the impact of their training programs.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
text:
🧪 Sample Characteristics
This meta-analysis reviewed 89 emperical studies published between 1988 and 2008 examining factors that influence how well training transfers to on-the-job performance. The studies, primarily from the US and Canada (85%), included a mix of field research and lab experiments with participants ranging from students to managers and other employees. Using databases like PsycINFO and ERIC, the review focused on studies reporting a link between training transfer and variables such as age, gender, education, experience, cognitive ability, personality traits, motivation, work environment, and various learning outcomes (Blume et al., 2010).

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
section: 🦁 Key Trainee Characteristics for Effective Training Transfer
text:
🦁 Key Trainee Characteristics for Effective Training Transfer
Certain trainee characteristics play a significant role in training transfer:


Cognitive Ability: Cognitive ability (how quickly someone can learn and process information) has a moderate link to training success. This isn’t surprising, but it’s important to remember that it’s just one piece of the puzzle


Being Conscientious Helps: Individuals who are organized, responsible, and diligent (high in conscientiousness) are more likely to apply what they’ve learned, emphasizing the value of a learning environment that supports accountability and consistent effort.


Voluntary Participation is Key: When people choose to participate in training, they’re more likely to benefit. This underscores the importance of buy-in and making training relevant to employees’ needs.


Self-Efficacy and Motivation Matter Too: Having confidence in your ability to learn new skills and being motivated to learn also contribute to successful transfer, although to a slightly lesser extent than the factors above.


While the aforementioned trainee characteristics are influential in the transfer of training, neuroticism can hinder the process, which is perhaps unsurprising.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
section: 🏛️ The Power of the Work Environment
text:
🏛️ The Power of the Work Environment
The work environment plays a crucial role in whether training transfers or not:


A Supportive Environment is Essential: A strong “transfer climate,” where managers and colleagues actively encourage and support the application of new skills, is the most significant predictor of training transfer. Managers who prioritize learning alongside performance create safe spaces and opportunities for employees to practice newly acquired skills, fostering a culture where continuous development is valued.


Support and Removing Barriers Matter: Beyond encouragement, practical support from supervisors and peers including resources, combined with efforts to eliminate obstacles that hinder the use of new skills, plays a crucial role in successful training transfer.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
text:
🧠 Learning Outcomes
What trainees gain from the training itself also influences transfer:


Confidence and Knowledge: Trainees are unlikely to apply what they’ve learned if the training lacks practical takeaways or fails to effectively develop their skills and knowledge. Building their confidence and equipping them with actionable knowledge and skills are crucial for successful transfer, underscoring the importance of well-designed, impactful training programs.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
section: 🧐 Important Considerations for Training Design and Evaluation
text:
🧐 Important Considerations for Training Design and Evaluation
The meta-analysis also revealed some interesting nuances that training developer should keep in mind:

Timing of Measurement Matters: When evaluating training effectiveness, the timing of measurement is a key consideration. Measuring learned skills immediately or shortly after training results in higher scores compared to later assessments. Therefore, positive closing survey ratings don’t necessarily indicate successful transfer.
Who’s Doing the Evaluation Matters: The method of measuring training transfer—whether through self-assessment, supervisor evaluation, or objective measures—can significantly impact the findings. This is understandable, as self-assessments are susceptible to impression management and various biases.
Type of Skill Matters: The kind of skill being taught—whether it’s a closed skill like data analysis (which has well-defined steps and rules) or an open skill like team development (which depends more on judgment and adaptability)—can affect how well people apply what they’ve learned. For example, being good at problem-solving (cognitive ability) helps more with learning closed skills. On the other hand, factors like motivation and support from coworkers or managers are even more important for transferring open skills into the workplace.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
text:
📜 Key Takeaways for Practitioners

Develop Supportive Climate & Learning Culture: Create a supportive environment that encourages and rewards the application of new skills. This is the most important factor!
Boost Trainee Confidence and Motivation: Help trainees build confidence in their ability to apply what they learn and make sure they understand the value of the training. Provide a clear rationale for the training, outlining its impact on the organization and individual careers. Communication is Key!
Design Training That Leads to Real Learning: Ensure training effectively imparts knowledge and skills. Make use of available literature and incorporate evidence-based practices and proven pedagogical techniques to maximize learning outcomes.
Consider the Type of Skill and the Training Context: Tailor your approach based on whether you’re teaching a closed or open skill and the organizational context, including the timing and method of transfer evaluation.
Remember that Training is Just the Beginning: Follow-up and ongoing support are essential for maximizing the return on your training investment. Create opportunities for the employees to apply their newly learned skills.

title: Making Training Stick: Insights from a Meta-Analysis on Training Transfer
text:
🎬 Conclusion
Training empowers individuals and organizations to navigate a rapidly changing landscape. Yet, maximizing the return on investment requires a focus on transfer of training. Insights from leading research like Blume et al. (2010) pave the way for designing effective programs that bridge the gap between theory and practice, ultimately leading to a more skilled and adaptable workforce.

Factor analysis is one of the most important tools psychometricians use to understand latent constructs. Before we jump into the analysis itself, let’s take a step back and talk about what a latent construct even is (in case you are not familliar). A construct is a theoretical, abstract idea that we can’t directly measure. Most psychological things fall under this category—our emotions, thoughts, internal processes, motivations, attitudes… none of this is directly visible. That’s why we call them latent constructs (latent = hidden).
Even though we can’t observe a construct directly, we can infer it through things we can observe—like self-reported behaviors, responses to questionnaire items, performance on tasks, physiological signals, and so on.

text:
🔎 A Quick Example
Think about intelligence testing. “Intelligence” is not something we can see or touch. But we can observe things like quantitative reasoning, verbal reasoning, and problem-solving speed. By measuring those observable skills, we infer something about the latent construct of intelligence.
Now, yes—there’s a huge debate about what intelligence even is, whether it’s innate, how much it can change, and whether practice effects undermine certain definitions. That’s a conversation for another day. The point is: psychometric tests let us learn about latent factors through observable variables that are easy to measure. And once we measure them, we can evaluate reliability, validity, and use them to predict or understand all sorts of fun things in academic and applied settings.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 🌝 EFA vs. CFA: what’s the difference?
text:
🌝 EFA vs. CFA: what’s the difference?
There are two types of factor analysis:

Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA)
CFA is used when you already have a theory or hypothesis. You’re basically asking, “Does my data support the structure I expect?” You test whether the model you believe in can be reproduced using your observed data.


Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA)
EFA is used when you don’t have a strong theory yet. You explore the data to see how many factors best explain the relationships among your observed variables. It’s like asking: “What structure naturally emerges from these items?”
For example, imagine personality research didn’t exist yet. You write a ton of items that describe different behaviors and attitudes. You don’t know how many dimensions of personality there are, or what they are. You run EFA to see which items “hang together,” and maybe you discover several clusters of items. You then interpret and name those clusters—maybe you end up with something like Oppenness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.
Mathematically, EFA is asking: Can a smaller number of underlying factors explain the variance and correlations we see in these measured variables?
It’s really just statistics doing what it always does: trying to explain variation.

ANOVA: do different groups explain variance in an outcome?
Regression: do predictors explain variance in an outcome?
EFA: do latent factors explain variance in many observed variables? Same logic—different target.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 🙉 So where does PCA come in, and why is it a problem?
text:
🙉 So where does PCA come in, and why is it a problem?
Another technique commonly used in our field is Principal Components Analysis (PCA). It looks very similar to EFA, so similar that software (like SPSS) puts them under the same menu. Unfortunately, this causes a lot of researchers to confuse the two and accidentally use PCA when they meant to use EFA.
And the problem is widespread: In a review of two measurement journals across six years, 64% of papers used PCA, while only 33% used EFA (Osborne et al., 2008). PCA is simply easier to click, so people default to it even when it’s not appropriate. Let’s get clear about the difference.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
text:
The Key Distinction
Both PCA and EFA reduce data, but they do it for very different reasons.

EFA: modeling underlying causes
EFA assumes that latent factors cause the observed variables.
The idea is:
    Factor → Variables
Mathematically:




Source: Karen Grace-Martin, TheAnalysisFactor.com



PCA: creating weighted combinations
PCA assumes the variables create the components. No underlying psychological cause—just weighted math.
    Variables → Component
Mathematically:




Source: Karen Grace-Martin, TheAnalysisFactor.com

So PCA components are literally linear combinations of the observed variables—not latent constructs.
Note. Throughout this blog, I use the terms “item,” “variable,” and “observed variable” interchangeably, as they refer to the same concept.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 🤔 What makes them fundamentally different: the mathematical assumption
text:
🤔 What makes them fundamentally different: the mathematical assumption
The major difference is how each method treats variance:

EFA

The diagonal of the covariance matrix < 1
Because variance is split into shared and unique parts
The diagonal only contains shared variance (communalities)
Meaning: EFA assumes variables have unique variance and measurement error



PCA

The diagonal is constrained to be 1
Meaning it assumes each variable’s entire variance is shared with all other variables (aka items)
No measurement error, no unique variance
This is almost never true in real data

This is why PCA is not good for theory building. It doesn’t model latent constructs. It doesn’t account for measurement error. It just compresses variables.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 📜 So when should you use which?
text:
📜 So when should you use which?

Use EFA when

You want to discover latent constructs
You care about theory
You want to model measurement error
You’re building a scale
You’re doing psychometric work

(Use Principal Axis Factoring or Maximum Likelihood—not PCA—as your extraction method in SPSS.)


Use PCA when

You purely want to reduce the number of variables
You don’t care about underlying constructs
You want to avoid multicollinearity
You want fewer predictors for machine learning models
You’re trying to simplify a large dataset

PCA is great for data prep—but not for understanding psychological constructs.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
text:
🧠 Final Thoughts
EFA and PCA look similar, but they answer completely different questions. When we mix them up, we unintentionally do bad science—not because we want to, but because the software makes it too easy to click the wrong thing.
So let’s be intentional about the tools we use. If you’re trying to understand a psychological construct, stick with EFA. If you’re just trying to shrink a large set of variables for practical reasons, PCA can be your friend.

title: R You Ready? An I/O Psychologist’s Guide to R & Rstudio
text: In recent years, the R programming language emerged as the industry standard in social science research, owing to its robust statistical analysis tools, powerful data visualization capabilities, and a rich ecosystem of packages. Its open-source nature and emphasis on reproducibility further propelled its widespread adoption. This workshop, titled “R You Ready? An I/O Psychologist’s Guide to R and RStudio,” was tailored for both R novices and those seeking a refresher, focusing on the essential 20% of R syntax that facilitated 80% of data analysis tasks. Participants were introduced to the RStudio environment and fundamental R syntax, followed by hands-on sessions covering data transformation (dplyr), data visualization (ggplot2), statistical analyses (lm, stats), APA-style reporting (markdown, apa, papaja), and text mining (stringr, tidytext). The workshop concluded with collaborative problem-solving sessions to reinforce the concepts learned. The aim was to introduce students and practitioners to the power of R to carry out basic and advanced analyses, along with the capability to visualize and report findings.

Getting Started

Sorting Data
Sorting is often one of the first transformations you’ll perform. Here’s how to do it in base R and tidyverse.

Option 1: Base R
In base R, you can use the order() function to sort by one or more columns:

# Sort by age in ascending order
index <- order(df$Age) 
df <- df[index, ]



Option 2: Tidyverse
The arrange() function from dplyr is a more concise and readable option:

# Sort by multiple columns: Age (descending) and DailyRate (ascending)
df <- arrange(df, desc(Age), DailyRate)





Renaming Columns
Renaming columns is another frequent task, especially when preparing data for analysis or visualization.

Option 1: Base R
Use the colnames() function to rename specific columns:

# Rename the first column (age)
colnames(df)[1] <- "how_old"



Option 2: Tidyverse
The rename() function provides an intuitive way to rename columns:

# Rename "how_old" back to "age"
df <- rename(df, "age" = "how_old")





Filtering Data

# Filter rows where MaritalStatus is "Single" and MonthlyIncome > 10000

🎨 Tutorial #2 (Visuals)
We will use ggplot2 to create visually appealing scatterplots, apply faceting for multi-panel plots, and customize plots for better presentation. These techniques are essential for exploratory data analysis and communicating insights effectively.

Scatterplots in ggplot2
Scatterplots are a powerful way to visualize relationships between two continuous variables.
Here’s how to create a simple scatterplot of YearsAtCompany vs. TotalWorkingYears with points colored red:

# Basic scatterplot
ggplot(data = df) +
  geom_point(aes(x = YearsAtCompany, y = TotalWorkingYears), color = "Red")




This code plots YearsAtCompany on the x-axis and TotalWorkingYears on the y-axis with red points.

Adding Aesthetic Mappings
To add another dimension, such as coloring points by MaritalStatus, use the aes() function:

# Scatterplot with points colored by MaritalStatus
ggplot(data = df) +
  geom_point(aes(x = YearsAtCompany, y = TotalWorkingYears, color = MaritalStatus))








Faceting for Multi-Panel Plots
Faceting allows you to split the data into panels based on a categorical variable.

# Faceted scatterplot by JobLevel
ggplot(data = df) +
  geom_point(aes(x = YearsAtCompany, y = YearsInCurrentRole)) +
  facet_wrap(~JobLevel, nrow = 2)




This creates separate scatterplots for each level of JobLevel, arranged in two rows.



More Cusomization
For this section, we’ll use the built-in mpg dataset. To enhance a scatterplot, you can map multiple aesthetics (e.g., color and size), customize axis labels, and add a title:

# Load the dataset
data(mpg)

# Scatterplot with multiple aesthetics and customizations
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv, size = cty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + # Add points with transparency
  # Customize axis labels and plot titles
  labs(title = "Fuel Efficiency vs. Engine Displacement",
       x = "Engine Displacement (L)",
       y = "Highway MPG",
       color = "Drive Type",
       size = "City MPG") +
  # Apply a theme
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~class)




Here’s what this code does:

Aesthetics: Maps drv (drive type) to color and cty (city MPG) to point size.
Labels: Adds a title, and custom axis labels, and modifies the legend titles.
Theme: Applies a clean, white background theme (theme_bw()).
Faceting: Creates facets for each vehicle class.

title: What Are Data Structures? A Simple Introduction for Beginners
text:
When working with data, organizing, storing, and performing operations on it efficiently is key. This is where data structures come into play. In simple terms, a data structure is a way of organizing and managing data so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently.

🔄 Data Type vs. Data Structure
If you are reading this, you’re likely already familiar with data types such as int (integer), float (floating-point number), str (string), and bool (Boolean). These are the building blocks used to define the kind of data you’re working with. When you perform data cleaning or analysis, you often manipulate these primitive data types.
Data structures build on these basic data types to manage and organize data more effectively. Think of it like constructing a car: the raw materials like metal and plastic are akin to the primitive data types, while the car’s components, such as the engine, trunk, doors, and wheels, represent the data structures. In essence, data structures use data types to create organized frameworks that allow for efficient storage and operations on your data.


⚙️ Common Operations
Data structures are essential tools in programming because they allow you to store, organize, and manage data efficiently. Common operations performed with data structures include:

Insertion: Adding new elements.
Deletion: Removing existing elements.
Searching: Finding specific elements.
Accessing: Retrieving elements by their position or key.
Updating: Modifying existing elements.

While data types tell the computer what kind of data is being stored (e.g., integers, strings, floats), they do not inherently provide a way to store multiple values together or perform advanced operations. For managing multiple similar data points, data structures become invaluable.


💡 Why Use Data Structures?
If you have several similar pieces of data to store and manipulate later, using a data structure allows for organized and efficient operations. Here’s an example:


Example: Storing Student Grades
Imagine you have 5 students in a class who took a final exam. Their grades need to be stored for future calculations.

Without a Data Structure
Using only data types, you could store the grades in separate variables like this:
student1 = 85
student2 = 90
student3 = 78
student4 = 92
student5 = 88
This approach works but becomes cumbersome as the number of students increases. Operations like calculating the average grade or updating a grade require manual effort for each variable.


With a Data Structure (Array)
Instead, you can use an array to store the grades:
student_grades = [85, 90, 78, 92, 88]
Now you can perform operations more efficiently:
# Access a specific grade: Retrieve the second student's grade
second_grade = student_grades[1]  # Outputs 90

# Update a grade: Add extra credit to the third student's grade
student_grades[2] += 5  # Updates 78 to 83

# Calculate the average grade: Compute the average for all students
average_grade = sum(student_grades) / len(student_grades)  # Outputs 86.6

# Add a new student: Include another student's grade
student_grades.append(95)

# Remove a student: Remove the grade of a student who dropped out
student_grades.pop(1)  # Removes the second student's grade


With a Data Structure (Hash Table)
If you need to associate grades with student names for better clarity, a hash table (dictionary) works even better:
student_grades = {
    "Sijan": 85,
    "Bella": 90,
    "Alex": 78,
    "Taylor": 92,
    "Jordan": 88
}
With this structure:

Accessing a grade by name is straightforward:

bella_grade = student_grades["Bella"]  # Outputs 90

Updating grades is intuitive:

student_grades["Alex"] += 5  # Updates Alex's grade to 83

Adding or removing students is easy:

student_grades["Chris"] = 95  # Adds Chris with a grade of 95
del student_grades["Taylor"]  # Removes Taylor




🛠️ Common Data Structures
Understanding the unique characteristics of different data structures—whether they are ordered or unordered, and what operations they excel at—helps in selecting the best one for a given task.

Array: An ordered collection of elements, best for quick access and iteration.
Linked List: An ordered, dynamic structure where elements are linked, ideal for frequent insertions and deletions.
Trees: A hierarchical, ordered structure, excellent for representing hierarchical relationships and performing searches.
Hash Table: An unordered structure using key-value pairs, best for fast lookups and retrievals.
Heap: A specialized tree-based structure, great for efficient retrieval of the smallest or largest element.
Graphs: A network of nodes connected by edges, perfect for modeling relationships and performing pathfinding operations.



🔍 Data Structures vs. Abstract Data Types (ADT)
Even if you’re not very familiar with the different data structures I’ve mentioned, you’re likely familiar with Abstract Data Types (ADTs) like lists, sets, and dictionaries. ADTs essentially define the operations or functionalities you can perform on data, while data structures are the low-level implementations that make those operations possible. Using the car example again, the ADT represents the car’s functionalities—driving, braking, and steering—while the data structures are the specific building blocks like the engine, wheels, and frame that make those functionalities work. ADTs are high-level abstract concepts, while data structures are the concrete details that enable those concepts to function.
Knowing just the ADT and its functionality will take you a long way, and you don’t necessarily need to understand the underlying data structures to perform different tasks. For instance, a list can be implemented using either an array or a linked list. When you use the built-in list function, like my_list = [], you don’t need to know whether it’s implemented using an array or a linked list. However, understanding the underlying data structure can be important for optimizing performance, such as improving runtime or space complexity. This deeper understanding helps you make more efficient decisions when choosing how to implement solutions, especially when performance is critical.


🗂️ Common ADTs
Here are some common ADTs and the data structures used to implement them:

List: Array, Linked List
Stack: Array, Linked List
Queue: Array, Linked List, Circular Buffer
Deque: Array, Doubly Linked List
Set: Hash Table, BST
Bag: Array, Linked List
Priority Queue: Binary Heap, Fibonacci Heap
Dictionary: Hash Table, BST



🌍 Real World Applications
Different data structures are utilized in real-world applications to optimize performance, manage data efficiently, and solve complex problems. Here are some practical implementations of commonly used data structures:

Array: Arrays are used in applications like image processing and spreadsheets where data is stored in contiguous memory locations for quick access.
Linked List: Linked lists are utilized in web browsers to manage navigation history, allowing for easy forward and backward movement.
Stack: Stacks are implemented in function call management, as well as in undo/redo operations in text editors, following the Last In, First Out (LIFO) principle.
Queue: Queues are used in operating systems for task scheduling and in customer service systems to process requests in the order they arrive.
Set: Sets are applied in social media platforms to store unique user data, such as friend lists, without duplicates.
Hash Table: Hash tables are used in contact management systems to map a user’s name to their phone number for fast lookups.
Binary Search Tree (BST): BSTs are used in databases for fast searching, insertion, and deletion of sorted records.
Heap: Heaps are implemented in job scheduling systems to prioritize tasks based on urgency or importance.
Graph: Graphs are used to model networks like social media connections, transportation systems, and web pages.



💭 Conclusion
These are just a few examples of how data structures are applied in the real world, and there are countless other uses that I haven’t covered here. It took me some time to truly grasp the key differences between data structures and other data types. This brief introduction to data structures serves as a way for me to reinforce my own understanding and, hopefully, help others in the process.
Data structures are fundamental tools for organizing and managing data efficiently across various real-world applications. From simple structures like arrays and linked lists to more complex ones like hash tables and graphs, each data structure has its own purpose based on the specific problem you’re trying to solve. Understanding these practical applications enables us to select the right data structure, optimize performance, and tackle challenges more effectively.
If you found this post helpful or have any feedback, I’d love to hear your thoughts—feel free to leave a comment below!

title: So… What Do You Study Again? My Daily Struggle Explaining I/O Psychology to Strangers
text:
Every time someone asks me what I am going to school for, I brace myself—because I know what’s coming. I have to say this long string of academic gibberish that sounds made up even to me: Industrial-Organizational Psychology.
I don’t usually say “I/O Psychology,” because I don’t expect anyone outside my small academic bubble to know what the acronym means. And honestly, when I say “I/O,” anyone from a computer science background thinks I am talking about input/output. Attaching psychology to that makes it more confusing. To be fair, our acronym does us no favors.
So my “better” option is to say the whole thing: Industrial-Organizational Psychology. A mouthful. I can count on one hand the number of times someone has understood me the first time I’ve said it. Half the time, I have to repeat myself slower, and even then, it still feels somewhat pretentious. Like, who do I think I am, announcing both “industry” and “organization” in the same breath? Sometimes I wish I had just gone the clinical route—not because it was ever my first love in psychology or something I think I would be particularly good at, but because at least that title wouldn’t make me sound pretentious at the early onset of a conversation with a stranger.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
text:
Factor analysis is one of the most important tools psychometricians use to understand latent constructs. Before we jump into the analysis itself, let’s take a step back and talk about what a latent construct even is (in case you are not familliar). A construct is a theoretical, abstract idea that we can’t directly measure. Most psychological things fall under this category—our emotions, thoughts, internal processes, motivations, attitudes… none of this is directly visible. That’s why we call them latent constructs (latent = hidden).
Even though we can’t observe a construct directly, we can infer it through things we can observe—like self-reported behaviors, responses to questionnaire items, performance on tasks, physiological signals, and so on.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
text:
🔎 A Quick Example
Think about intelligence testing. “Intelligence” is not something we can see or touch. But we can observe things like quantitative reasoning, verbal reasoning, and problem-solving speed. By measuring those observable skills, we infer something about the latent construct of intelligence.
Now, yes—there’s a huge debate about what intelligence even is, whether it’s innate, how much it can change, and whether practice effects undermine certain definitions. That’s a conversation for another day. The point is: psychometric tests let us learn about latent factors through observable variables that are easy to measure. And once we measure them, we can evaluate reliability, validity, and use them to predict or understand all sorts of fun things in academic and applied settings.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 🌝 EFA vs. CFA: what’s the difference?
text:
🌝 EFA vs. CFA: what’s the difference?
There are two types of factor analysis:

Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA)
CFA is used when you already have a theory or hypothesis. You’re basically asking, “Does my data support the structure I expect?” You test whether the model you believe in can be reproduced using your observed data.


Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA)
EFA is used when you don’t have a strong theory yet. You explore the data to see how many factors best explain the relationships among your observed variables. It’s like asking: “What structure naturally emerges from these items?”
For example, imagine personality research didn’t exist yet. You write a ton of items that describe different behaviors and attitudes. You don’t know how many dimensions of personality there are, or what they are. You run EFA to see which items “hang together,” and maybe you discover several clusters of items. You then interpret and name those clusters—maybe you end up with something like Oppenness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.
Mathematically, EFA is asking: Can a smaller number of underlying factors explain the variance and correlations we see in these measured variables?
It’s really just statistics doing what it always does: trying to explain variation.

ANOVA: do different groups explain variance in an outcome?
Regression: do predictors explain variance in an outcome?
EFA: do latent factors explain variance in many observed variables? Same logic—different target.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 🙉 So where does PCA come in, and why is it a problem?
text:
🙉 So where does PCA come in, and why is it a problem?
Another technique commonly used in our field is Principal Components Analysis (PCA). It looks very similar to EFA, so similar that software (like SPSS) puts them under the same menu. Unfortunately, this causes a lot of researchers to confuse the two and accidentally use PCA when they meant to use EFA.
And the problem is widespread: In a review of two measurement journals across six years, 64% of papers used PCA, while only 33% used EFA (Osborne et al., 2008). PCA is simply easier to click, so people default to it even when it’s not appropriate. Let’s get clear about the difference.

The Key Distinction
Both PCA and EFA reduce data, but they do it for very different reasons.

EFA: modeling underlying causes
EFA assumes that latent factors cause the observed variables.
The idea is:
    Factor → Variables

EFA

PCA: creating weighted combinations
PCA assumes the variables create the components. No underlying psychological cause—just weighted math.
    Variables → Component
Mathematically:




PCA

So PCA components are literally linear combinations of the observed variables—not latent constructs.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 🤔 What makes them fundamentally different: the mathematical assumption
text:
🤔 What makes them fundamentally different: the mathematical assumption
The major difference is how each method treats variance:

EFA

The diagonal of the covariance matrix < 1
Because variance is split into shared and unique parts
The diagonal only contains shared variance (communalities)
Meaning: EFA assumes variables have unique variance and measurement error



PCA

The diagonal is constrained to be 1
Meaning it assumes each variable’s entire variance is shared with all other variables (aka items)
No measurement error, no unique variance
This is almost never true in real data

This is why PCA is not good for theory building. It doesn’t model latent constructs. It doesn’t account for measurement error. It just compresses variables.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
section: 📜 So when should you use which?
text:
📜 So when should you use which?

Use EFA when

You want to discover latent constructs
You care about theory
You want to model measurement error
You’re building a scale
You’re doing psychometric work

(Use Principal Axis Factoring or Maximum Likelihood—not PCA—as your extraction method in SPSS.)


Use PCA when

You purely want to reduce the number of variables
You don’t care about underlying constructs
You want to avoid multicollinearity
You want fewer predictors for machine learning models
You’re trying to simplify a large dataset

PCA is great for data prep—but not for understanding psychological constructs.

title: Your Data Deserves Better: Understanding When to Use EFA or PCA
text:
🧠 Final Thoughts
EFA and PCA look similar, but they answer completely different questions. When we mix them up, we unintentionally do bad science—not because we want to, but because the software makes it too easy to click the wrong thing.
So let’s be intentional about the tools we use. If you’re trying to understand a psychological construct, stick with EFA. If you’re just trying to shrink a large set of variables for practical reasons, PCA can be your friend.

title: So… What Do You Study Again? My Daily Struggle Explaining I/O Psychology to Strangers
text:
Every time someone asks me what I am going to school for, I brace myself—because I know what’s coming. I have to say this long string of academic gibberish that sounds made up even to me: Industrial-Organizational Psychology.
I don’t usually say “I/O Psychology,” because I don’t expect anyone outside my small academic bubble to know what the acronym means. And honestly, when I say “I/O,” anyone from a computer science background thinks I am talking about input/output. Attaching psychology to that makes it more confusing. To be fair, our acronym does us no favors.
So my “better” option is to say the whole thing: Industrial-Organizational Psychology. A mouthful. I can count on one hand the number of times someone has understood me the first time I’ve said it. Half the time, I have to repeat myself slower, and even then, it still feels somewhat pretentious. Like, who do I think I am, announcing both “industry” and “organization” in the same breath? Sometimes I wish I had just gone the clinical route—not because it was ever my first love in psychology or something I think I would be particularly good at, but because at least that title wouldn’t make me sound pretentious at the early onset of a conversation with a stranger.

And honestly, the title is just the first hurdle. The next (and worse) hurdle is the inevitable follow-up question: “What the hell is that?” if the person is polite, which is often the case: “Tell me more about what that means.” At this point, I almost prefer people assuming I provide therapy to stressed-out employees. At least that sounds tangible— even if I am nowhere near qualified for that profession.
When I first started grad school, the “tell me more” question used to absolutely expose me. In my head, I would be thinking: Sir, I’m still trying to figure that out myself—how do you expect me to explain it to you? I would mumble something like “Well, it’s a lot of things… there’s the industrial side… and then the organizational side…” and then I would start naming random popular constructs like job satisfaction and organizational commitment. By the end of my explanation, they had learned absolutely nothing. I think a lot of management consultants can relate—the more indescribable your work sounds, the cooler people assume your work is. Maybe that’s why academic writing is so unnecessarily complex: so we can feel good about ourselves for producing sentences which can be comprehended only by people with certain training (I’m joking… mostly)
But jokes aside, those conversations always started off awkward, not because the field is complicated, but because I tended to over-explain. Most people just want the gist. And I have realized that trying to sound cool or impressive actually gets in the way of building real connections. So, I have been working on simplifying how I describe what I do—without losing what makes it meaningful.

title: Fairness at Work: More Than Objective System, It’s Perception
text:
Out of all the constructs we love to discuss in I/O Psychology, perceptions of justice—or simply, fairness perception—speaks to me on a personal level. Growing up in Bangladesh, fairness wasn’t just an abstract idea—it was woven into our history. If you’ve taken a course called multilevel modeling, you know why we compare people within their own reference groups. Context matters, and mine shaped how I see justice.
My parents, like many in South Asia, carried a quiet anxiety rooted in generations of injustice and uncertainty. There’s an old Sanskrit saying, Atithi Devo Bhava—“Guests are gods” so we treat them as such. We welcomed the British as guests, happily trading spices… until they overstayed a couple extra centuries on their guest pass. Lesson learned: vet them out before you let them in. A practice that is popular in American visa offices across the globe.
Fast forward to 1947. East Bengal became part of Pakistan. It was supposed to be the happy ending, but happy endings tend to show up a little less often outside of movies. Our fellow Pakistani “brothers” treated East Bengal like a step-sibling asking for their fair share of the family inheritance. We had less opportunity, less funding, less of just about everything—and on top of that, we were told to switch our mother tongue and culture to fit into a country that didn’t consider us equals. So, naturally, we fought back—for our rights, for the fairness we hold dear—and in 1971, Bangladesh was born.
That history shaped our values: be cautious, be fair, be just. Even my alma mater, Jhenidah Cadet College, drilled this into us with its motto: The learned are judicious. So yes—fairness is personal to me. And when I entered graduate school and learned how perceptions of justice influence morale, commitment, and performance, something clicked. I understood why people in Bangladesh take to the streets—not from jealousy, but for their rights, because they believe the system has failed them, and they respond to systems they perceive as unfair. We’re all dealt different cards at birth; the least we can ask for is a fair system. That’s when I found my calling: building systems that are just, valid, and reliable. Psychometrics became my language; data science became my toolbox.
While I could happily spend hours diving into statistics and measurement, I will leave that for another time. Instead, I would like to focus on organizational justice for the rest of this blog—what it looks like in the workplace, how it affects employees, and why organizations should care—illustrating the construct through examples and research findings.

title: Fairness at Work: More Than Objective System, It’s Perception
text:
⚖️ Breaking down Organizational Justice
In the workplace, “justice” isn’t just one thing. Researchers generally break it into four types:

Distributive Justice: This is about fairness in outcomes. Three classic principles guide it: 1) Equity: rewards match contributions. 2) Equality: everyone gets the same. 3) Need: those who need more receive more (Huang et al., 2017)
Procedural Justice: This focuses on how decisions are made. Were rules applied consistently? Was bias minimized? Was the process based on accurate, relevant information? (Huang et al., 2017)
Interpersonal Justice: This is about how people are treated—respect, politeness, dignity (Bies, 2015). Small behaviors, big impact.
Informational Justice: This relates to the quality of communication: Was information shared honestly, thoroughly, equally, and at the right time? (Greenberg, 1993).

Now, why does all this matter? Because these layers operate in our minds even when we can’t quite articulate what feels “off”, quietly influencing our mood, motivation, performance and wellbeing.

Take distributive justice:
Imagine you land your dream job. You get along with everyone, you’re paid well—but then you find out a coworker received a bigger bonus despite having the same contributions. Or you stay long after office hours and put in extra work during the weekend, yet everyone gets the same end-of-year reward. Your perception—not the objective policy—drives how you feel.


Or consider procedural justice:
When a high-visibility project opens up, you want the selection process to be based on merit—not on who plays golf with the boss. If you think the system is rigged, your motivation slips. The bottom line: when employees sense unfairness, everything else starts to unravel.

title: Fairness at Work: More Than Objective System, It’s Perception
section: 👀 Why Perception of Fairness Matters More Than You Think
text:
👀 Why Perception of Fairness Matters More Than You Think
A highly motivated employee can quickly disengage if they believe the system favors some over others. That’s how quiet quitting begins. That’s why Gen Z switches jobs faster than soccer players switch hairstyles—when people sense unfairness, they leave.
And turnover is expensive. Depending on the role, replacing an employee can cost anywhere from 30% to 150% of their salary (G&A Partners, 2024). Redistribution of workload, recruitment, onboarding—it all adds up. Worse, if your hiring system is biased, you might end up with a false positive—a bad fit who costs you even more.

Research backs this up:
When employees perceive injustice, they often reciprocate through reduced effort or even counterproductive behaviors such as theft, withdrawal, or intentionally slowing work (Rupp et al., 2014). Justice perceptions shape who employees blame for unfairness and how they respond.


But the reverse is also true:
Employees who feel fairly treated show stronger job attitudes, better performance, and higher organizational commitment (Colquitt et al., 2001; Rupp et al., 2014). They brag about their company, act generously toward coworkers, and become ambassadors on social media—driving talent and customers your way.

title: Fairness at Work: More Than Objective System, It’s Perception
text:
🚨 Bottom Line
Fairness or the perception of it isn’t a “nice-to-have.” It’s a strategic advantage. Organizations that take justice seriously—not only in objective policies but also in how those policies feel to employees—avoid costly turnover, boost morale, and cultivate healthier workplaces.
And honestly, who wouldn’t want to work for a company that not only treats people fairly but also ensures they perceive it that way?

title: The Central Limit Theorem: The Principle at the Heart of Statistics and Data Thinking
text:
The theory of theories—the one that quietly rules the statistical universe—is the Central Limit Theorem. This isn’t an exaggeration; it’s one of the few ideas that has genuinely stood the test of time—one that every researcher and statistician owes a debt to. Although the theorem was being used as far back as the early 1800s, the name Central Limit Theorem (CLT) didn’t appear until the 1920s, thanks to George Pólya. And honestly, he nailed it. Since then, the CLT has truly become the center of our world, proving that its title was both accurate and unintentionally poetic.
Think of learning the CLT as the equivalent of learning the alphabet for statisticians. If you don’t understand the alphabet, you can’t read. And if you don’t understand the CLT, you can’t interpret data in any meaningful way. It’s the foundation for everything—from the simplest tests like t-tests and ANOVAs to the most complex models, including multilevel modeling and machine learning algorithms.

section: 🌎 Making Sense of the Messy World Around Us
text:
🌎 Making Sense of the Messy World Around Us
Let’s imagine you and your friend group believe that staying up all night watching TikTok makes you smarter. You’re learning new things, absorbing information you wouldn’t have learned if you were asleep — so it must be good, right?
Sure… maybe in your friend group.
But is it universally true? Do people across different ages, cultures, and backgrounds share that belief? Or is your friend group just an extreme case?
Naturally, we cannot ask all 8 billion people on Earth. So how can we ever truly know that if something is universally true across the entire population or at least a subsection of it? That’s where the CLT comes in.
If we surveyed a huge number of people about this belief and plotted the results, the histogram might take any shape:




Source: Kahadawala Cooray, Exponentiated Sinh Cauchy Distribution with Applications


It might look like a bell curve (if most people are somewhere in the middle).

People’s height
Test scores on a reasonably challenging exam






Source: Kahadawala Cooray, Exponentiated Sinh Cauchy Distribution with Applications


It might be skewed (if most people strongly disagree or if there are only a few extreme values).

Income (a classic right-skew)
Time spent on social media (many low users, a few very heavy users)






Source: Kahadawala Cooray, Exponentiated Sinh Cauchy Distribution with Applications


It might even be weirdly shaped (because humans are weirdly shaped in their opinions).

Political ideology in a polarized environment (bimodal: clusters on the left and right)
Daily caffeine consumption (clusters of non-drinkers, 1-cup people, and “five-cups-before-8am” people)



🪄 But here’s the magical part:
No matter what the original distribution looks like—bell-shaped, skewed, or downright weird—the Central Limit Theorem says something remarkable.


Central Limit Theorem:  If you take repeated random samples, compute their averages, and then plot those averages (the sample means), the distribution of those sample means will form a normal, bell-shaped curve.
And the center of that bell? It will land right on the true population mean—or extremely close to it.

Note. I know, that’s a lot of “means” and “averages,” but read it twice and let it sink in. It’s worth it.
Because this idea is huge. It means we can understand something about an entire population without surveying every single person. It means we can make strong, probability-based statements from just a random, representative sample.
Why? Because once we have that bell-shaped distribution of sample means, we know exactly how the probabilities behave around it—the classic rule: 68% between ±1 SD, 95% between ±2 SD, 99.7% between ±3 SD.

In other words: statistics works because the CLT works.
And once we have that predictable bell curve, we can use it to answer our most desired questions, like:

Is your friend group’s belief unusual?

Maybe you and your friends are convinced that pulling all-nighters makes you smarter. But if you looked at a random group of people from different ages, backgrounds, and cultures, would their average opinion be the same as yours?

Is the difference meaningful?

Maybe your sample shows that heavy late-night TikTok users feel more creative the next day. But is that difference large compared to what we’d expect by chance, or would most samples show something similar?


That famous 5% cutoff (p < .05), while admittedly arbitrary, is built entirely on this idea.
If your sample statistic—say, the average belief of your friend group—falls in the most extreme 5% of the sampling distribution (the far tails of that bell curve), then the odds that it came from a world where “nothing special is happening” are pretty slim.
In about 95% of samples, the confidence interval we construct will contain the true population parameter. So when your sample lands way outside the center, it signals that something meaningful might be going on.
Maybe your group is exposed to something the rest of the population isn’t—like:

Algorithms that feed you more educational TikToks because of your viewing history
Higher levels of curiosity or openness, making you more likely to interpret TikTok as educational

title: The magic in our nature: The e
text:
🪄 Why Is “e” a Magical Number?
Becasue e shows up everywhere—in population growth, disease spread, radioactive decay, loan payments, physics, biology, and even in your savings account. It’s called natural because it appears naturally in any process where something keeps growing or changing a little bit at a time. That’s why it’s at the core of calculus (the math of growth).
But you don’t need calculus to understand it. The easiest way to feel its magic is through compound interest.

Compound Interest Example
Imagine you have $1, and a miracle bank gives you 100% interest per year.

Case 1: Interest once per year

You start with $1
100% interest → you end with $2 Easy.



Case 2: Interest twice per year
Instead of 100% once, the bank gives:

50% after 6 months
50% after another 6 months
Your money becomes: \((1 + \tfrac{1}{2})^2 = \$2.25\)



Case 3: Interest every month (12 times)



Your money becomes \(\approx\) 2.613

\((1 + \tfrac{1}{12})^{12} \approx 2.613\)

More compounding → more growth.



Case 4: Interest every day (365 times)



Your money becomes \(\approx\) 2.714

\((1 + \tfrac{1}{365})^{365} \approx 2.714\)

Even closer to something…



Case 5: Interest every second

(365 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes × 60 seconds) = 31,536,000 seconds


Your money becomes \(\approx\) 2.71828

\((1 + \tfrac{1}{31{,}536{,}000})^{31{,}536{,}000} \approx 2.71828\)

Your ending amount gets a tiny bit bigger—but not by much.



Case 6: Interest infinitely often

Now imagine compounding faster and faster, without stopping.
As we increase the number of times we compound:

the final amount keeps rising
but it rises slower and slower


and it settles down to a very specific number \(\approx\) 2.7182881828…

\(\lim_{n \to \infty} (1 + \tfrac{1}{n})^{n} = 2.718281828…\)




That number is e.










What’s amazing is this:
You can compound interest as fast as you want— every year, every month, every day, every second— and the result will never go above e.

That limit—the maximum possible money you can get from 100% growth over one period—that number is e. e is what happens when you push compounding interest to the absolute limit.

This is why this number is called natural. It’s literally baked into how growth behaves in our universe. And we are not only talking about money growth, growth of population, disease and every other things follows this. Everything grows in the exponent of this natural e.

Once you accept that continuously compounding 100% interest gives you \(e\), you can generalize it.

Instead of a 100% growth rate (\(r = 1\)), what if your rate is \(r\)?
Instead of 1 year, what if your time is \(t\) years?

That’s where this formula comes into play:
\[
\Huge e^{rt}
\]
Where:

\(r\) = growth rate
\(t\) = number of time periods

Example: If you have a 200% growth rate (\(r = 2\)) for 5 years (\(t = 5\)):
\[
e^{rt} = e^{2*5} = e^{10}
\]
This is why \(e\) shows up everywhere—finance, biology, psychology, machine learning—anywhere something grows or changes continuously.

Maybe your sample shows that heavy late-night TikTok users feel more creative the next day. But is that difference large compared to what we’d expect by chance, or would most samples show something similar?
